passage: Evening note from Himani. Today my daughter Pallavi sat with my mother while Nani explained why the pickle jar must be dried in the sun before it is closed. Pallavi did not interrupt once. She nodded and watched Nani's hands. Then she asked, quite gently, "Nani, why does the jar have to be dry?" Nani said water lets mould grow, and that her own mother had taught her, and that she learned it the hard way when one jar spoiled. Pallavi said, "So that is why. Can I turn the jars with you tomorrow?" I stayed out of it. I noticed I was proud, and that Nani looked happy to be asked.

qa.q: What did Nani say must be done to the pickle jar before it is closed?
qa.a: She said it must be dried in the sun.

qa.q: What did Pallavi feel toward Nani as she listened, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She listened without interrupting and then gently asked why, and she asked to help the next day, which shows respect and curiosity together.

qa.q: How could Himani support this kind of listening at home?
qa.a: Himani could keep stepping back and invite Nani to share more of what Nani has learned, while letting Pallavi ask questions.

qa.q: What might Nani have felt when Pallavi asked why?
qa.a: She probably felt valued, since the question showed Pallavi cared about the experience behind the advice, and Himani noticed Nani looked happy.

grounding: A child listens to a grandmother without interrupting and still politely asks why.
